title: Segregation and the full touring route
summary: Venues were black until integration, though auditorium shows were mixed; he describes a route through Florida, Alabama, Louisiana and Texas.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Were these basically black clubs or would you play a mix? Yeah.

They was black until, they was, well see, I'm in fun way back. Of course now they all mixed, you know, since the integration bill passed, they all mixed, you see. Right. But in them days it was all black, you see.
But we'd like you to get an auditorium show.

Well, even in old days back then, did an auditorium show, they would mix it because the integration bill hadn't passed, you see. We was playing a lot of fraternities, sororities, you know, which was all white, you know. Yeah. But now it's all, you know, later down the line after the bill passed, everything got different. We played both white and black, you see. Same way with school prong. We played school prong, used to be all black, now we play a white and black school prong, you see. And we'd play into Pensacola, down to Fort Wallen Beach, and out of Fort Wallen Beach we'd go into Panama City, and out of Panama City we'd come back into Dothan, Alabama. See, we had a real route set up, you know. And on back then to Alabama, we'd come back then to the Merida, Mississippi, and on from Merida down to Hattiesburg and back in the New Orleans. And then maybe next time we'd go on a trip, we'd go into Baton Rouge, into Alexander, and Alexander into Monroe, and out of Monroe into Memphis. And we'd hit Lake, Lifeyette, Opelousa, we'd hit Opelousa, Lake, Lifeyette, Lake Charles, and Beaumont, Texas, into Houston. We had a real route, we'd know why, we had clubs waiting for us to call them. You know, we had a pretty good set up, you know. Right. This month we might travel from here into Florida, into Alabama, back to Mississippi, into New Orleans, and the next month we might start traveling from Baton Rouge into Hopelousa, into Lyfeeette, to Lake Charles, Beaumont, into Houston, you see. Sometime we'd go up as far as San Antonio, because we got a big, uh, two big fields there. They got Fort Sam Houston and uh, yeah, Fort Sam Houston, you see. Of course, now we had contacts, we had guys that was working parts, you know. They'd say, you, you live in that town, so I'll tell you I got four or five nights open on so-and-so's, and you, I'll take the four or five nights here, I'll bomb, or we take them together. Yeah. Most of the time we'd play together because they'd more money, you see. Yeah. We'd put more money down, just pay the artists and things off, you see. So that's what we really worked. And it was a pretty good thing.
